title: What Oppenheimer Really Thought About the Atomic Bomb
the_thought: He thought he had built a thing so terrible that using it again would end the world.
hook: Before dawn in July 1945, Robert Oppenheimer crouched in a control bunker in the New Mexico desert and waited for a sunrise he had built himself. For three years he had driven thousands of people to make this weapon first. Then, for the rest of his life, he fought to keep anyone from ever using one again. Why? He thought he had built a thing so terrible that using it again would end the world. So why did the man who came to fear the bomb build the most powerful one on Earth?

levels.name: The Fear
beats: The answer starts with a fear. In the last weeks of 1938, scientists in Berlin split the atom on a laboratory bench. If that discovery could be turned into a bomb, the country most likely to do it first was Nazi Germany. Oppenheimer was a dazzling, restless theorist who had never run anything bigger than a seminar. Yet a blunt Army engineer named General Groves picked him to lead a secret city in the mountains of New Mexico. He said yes at once. Years later he tried to explain the pull of the work. When you see something that is technically sweet, he said, you go ahead and do it. He believed the safest hands for such a weapon were the first hands to hold it.

levels.name: The Test
beats: By the summer of 1945, Germany had already surrendered. The enemy they had feared was gone, but the bomb was nearly finished, so the work rolled on. They hauled the gadget, a round steel shell bristling with cables, up a hundred-foot tower on a plain the old Spanish maps called the Journey of the Dead Man. Oppenheimer gave the test a quiet, haunting name: Trinity. In the final minutes, a few scientists joked about whether the blast might set the sky itself on fire. At twenty-nine minutes past five, the darkness became a light no human had ever seen. Watching it, one line from an ancient poem rose in his mind. Now, he thought, he had become Death, the destroyer of worlds.

levels.name: The Cities
beats: Three weeks later, the weapon was no longer a test. On the sixth of August, a single bomb destroyed most of Hiroshima. Three days after that, a second fell on Nagasaki. At the lab, scientists cheered, and Oppenheimer stepped onto the stage and clasped his hands above his head like a winning boxer. Yet something had already curdled in him. That autumn he sat with President Truman and said, almost in a whisper, that he felt he had blood on his hands. Truman was revolted. He later told his staff never to bring that cry-baby scientist into his office again. The man who made the bomb and the man who ordered its use could no longer bear the sight of each other.

levels.name: The Reversal
beats: From that point on, Oppenheimer used his enormous fame to try to put the weapon back in its box. He argued that no wall of secrecy could hold such a thing for long, and that real safety lay in openness between nations. When his government wanted a hydrogen bomb, a weapon a thousand times stronger, he led the panel that warned it could become an instrument of genocide. Powerful men never forgave him. In 1954, in a small, locked room, the country put its own bomb-maker on trial and quietly stripped away his secret clearance. Around then he said a sentence that has never stopped echoing. In some crude sense, he said, the physicists have known sin, and that is a knowledge they cannot lose.

levels.name: The Last One
beats: So what did he truly believe the bomb was for? Near the end he offered an image no one who heard it forgot. Two great nations armed with these weapons, he said, were like two scorpions in a bottle, each able to kill the other only at the price of its own life. He didn't think the bomb had made his country safe. He thought it had made everyone a prisoner of the same fear. He had raced to build it because he dreaded who might build it first. By the end, he was certain of one thing. He thought he had built a thing so terrible that using it again would end the world.

But he wasn't the only mind who helped unlock the atom and then recoiled from it. The physicist who first imagined the nuclear chain reaction spent years trying to chain his own idea back down, and that is a story for another time.
